So unlike kind of any other area of the State, you have state, and with layers of local law that's, that's preventing big subdivisions and development projects. We have seen like, there is a development project in Freeport. That's just outside the Delta. I don't know if you've, you should take a look at it from the aerial. But just on the back side of Freeport, they're putting in like 2,000 homes or something. It's crazy. But you know, that's just outside. So if you look at the map and you see where the development's being proposed, it's outside of the Delta, because the Delta Protection Commission administers the, what's the name of that? There, they have the land use management plan, and it doesn't allow for, you know, for, you know, there's certain, you can do some farm related. So you've got the big Bogle processing facility, for instance, down Jefferson Road. So there's things like that can happen. But in terms of developing cities, it's not gonna happen. So the cool thing about that is that it's going to maintain, repeat, stay in agriculture. Right? If we can continue to have an adequate water supply of a decent quality, like was promised to the farmers when the State and Federal water projects were, were built, you know, then, and like the, the water right system, I think, requires, I mean, to the extent it's feasible. So that's what's kind of my whole hang up with the just transitions ideas. I felt that, editorializing a little here, is that there's a big push by folks who are responsible for maintaining salinity in the Delta to try to show that, oh, it's just not possible anymore. It's like, well, I don't think that's an option. And you know, we have to change Federal and State law to take away the obligations that were entered into, now, anyway, well, I'll let, we'll get into the other questions. But I just, you know, that's kind of my position on that. I don't. I don't think it's appropriate to be saying like, oh, yeah, you know, this place is going to hell in a handbasket, you know. See you later. You know I don't think we say that, you know, like you told that to people in Holland, or like, you know again, the people of the area end up being kind of invisible. But, you know they shouldn't be, because when would it be okay to say like, yeah, see ya. You know, you, you can't be there anymore. I mean, obviously, people have to pay fair share for flood protection and other things they need. It can't be like a big handout situation, but I don't think it is, and I think you know, that's, that, you know. That's kind of the challenge into the future is how to, you know, have that right balance of investments to protect statewide important infrastructure, and then also, locally important infrastructure. And you know, it, it takes. It's gonna take, you know, everybody working together to to make that happen.

background.speaker: AD
background.content: I'm curious, and I don't know much about this, but, the difference in how, like that viewpoint that you just expressed about the Delta, and saying like, oh well, versus protecting our coastlines from erosion and other coastline management? And like I said, I don't know much about coastline management. That's not what I've studied. But do you see a difference? Because I mean, like you said you can't just tell people, oh, well, you can't live here anymore, I don't, I assume, which may be incorrect and please correct me if I'm wrong, but I assume no one's telling people on, you know, coastal properties, oh, well, you just can't live here anymore. Your house is just gonna fall into the ocean.

background.speaker: OM
background.content: Well, I think there was a story last week, and I think it was last week where the Coastal Commission is saying like, yeah, you can't get a coastal development permit to build a seawall or other structures that might, that the landowners might consider to be necessary to protect their, their home, say, from, you know, erosion. So that is happening on the coast. And the State saying, like, hey, we're, we're not gonna do this. I mean, I think, luckily for, for the Delta, there's a couple of differences, one of which is, you know, the, for, you know, we don't have a big like erosion issue per se, right? And, and the sea level rise to date has been quite minimal, you know. And, there's also an issue that gets overlooked quite a bit is that to the extent there, I mean, the problem with the Golden Gate is apparently, and I'm trying to do like a little fact sheet about this, so if I finish it ,when I finish it I'll, I'll give it to you. But. They've had a bunch of problems with the gauges on the Golden Gate, and whatnot, too. So like where they were trying to measure, you know, and say, like, oh, is the sea level risen, you know, how much since 1850, say. They don't really know cause they screwed up, or maybe it was, you know, an accident, but they don't, and again, it's tidal, too, right? So you're looking at like average. But I mean, I think at the Golden Gate, sea level has potentially gone up, you know, a matter of maybe a couple of inches in the past 150 or… 1850, …174 years or so. So I mean it's, which is not to say we know what will happen over the next 10 years. But I mean it's not as dramatic as you might think, you know. And then, in addition, the farther away you move from the Golden Gate, there's a lot of attenuation. So that's the other thing that kind of gets lost. And people start talking about like, oh, they're gonna be sucking salt water out the South Delta pumps. No, I mean, you know, it probably has incrementally gotten a little saltier. A lot of that's because the crap coming down the San Joaquin River is so full of salts from going through those farmlands that are compromised already, and how selenium and all these other things on the west side, what we call the West Side. So. It's not necessarily because of sea level rise. So there's, you know, I mean, I think, for purposes of public information and taking global warming seriously, there's a lot of like, tools you can look at where it's like, okay, well, look at what would happen with one foot of sea level rise or something, right? And it shows Elk Grove underwater. That's not gonna happen. I mean, I'm not saying it couldn't ever happen. But, that doesn't take into account the attenuation. So sometimes these tools that are used for educational purposes to kind of like wake people up or make people more aware of a problem, like they are, you know, they're, they're oversimplifying. So like one thing you'll want to look at, too like is Ocean Protection Commission just put out a new Ocean Protection Council. They just came up, they just put out a new advisory about sea level rise, where they completely retracted the 1.8 foot sea level rise by 2050 that they had suggested we ought to be planning around. They, they took that back and said that it wasn't based on sound science and it, and this is something we had said, too, was like, look, that, according to the docs, you were looking at, the studies, it had a 0.05% chance of occurring. The inches of sea level rise that had a 66% chance of occurring was like, I think, 6 inches by 2050. Anyway, I mean, don't quote me, but like it. And again, it's not to say we don't need to plan for sea level rise but, you know, this kind of the sky is falling type mentality is not helpful, you know, in terms of actually planning, and some, and some entities, like the State water contractors, I would say, and the Federal water contractors are using it as a, as a reason to get rid of the water quality standards and their obligation to release from storage, which they're holding holding back so. And I guess the the second thing that's different from the example of the, you know, homes along the shore and the ocean is that we have the ability to to widen and raise our levees, to deal with sea level rise and, and what we're trying to do is get on a pathway where we can get all the levees up to a kind of minimum standard. And into this fat levee situation. Where then, as sea level, does rise, assuming it does, that we can build on top of that as we go. So you don't need to build, you know, 50 foot levee right now, and hopefully never need to do one that high. But you know, you can basically set it up from an engineering perspective where you're kind of ready to continue going. And like, for instance, I had a [redacted] I worked on a while, many years ago in [redacted], where I was actually working for [redacted]. And [redacted] was like, hey, you need to raise the sea- these levees up to, you know, 10 feet high, or whatever it was. And we're like, yeah, we'll just make them so they're good enough for now, and they're wide enough, and then every 5 years we will assess what's going on with the best available scientific information, and then we'll add to it as needed to continue to have what, I think in that case was 200 year flood protection. So, I mean, I'm not saying it has to be that standard, but that's the good thing about levees is that they actually, you know, people talk about crumbling dirt levies and stuff is kind of stupid. It's like, yeah. Levees are made out of dirt. Like, what do you expect? You know? Anyway.

background.speaker: AD
background.content: Alright, thank you, yeah, that, it's very, interesting I wrote down a couple of things to look up from that. So thank you. How have you, how have you been impacted by salinity in the Delta? And you can answer this personally or professionally, or both.

background.speaker: OM
background.content: I mean, I think what I'm concerned about for [redacted] is that there's been in, incremental increases in salinity sometimes because the State Water Board allows it under the temporary urgency change process. And we think it probably, that that shouldn't be done for the projects. The projects need to plan for 5 years or more of drought with respect to their storage. But, it's, it has a, it basically reduces agricultural productivity, because you end up with salt buildup in the root zone. Right? And so. One of the… There's a specialist, which I think that you probably have been in, [redacted]. She's a [redacted]. I'm blanking on her name, but she has done a lot of studies about this issue, because a lot of times people are like, oh yeah, you could just leach out the salt by, like, you know with more water. Well, if you have a high groundwater table, which we do in the Delta, you can't just leach it out, so. And there's this whole thing called a leaching fraction. And all this stuff which I learned about a bit. But. So that's my concern is that over time, increasing salinity, even if incremental, starts reducing your agricultural productivity, which in the Delta, and you don't have a good chance to try to leach out those salts. So that's a concern that I have with increasing salinity. And then just, it doesn't seem like the State Water Board is as protective of, you know, when they balance the interests, they typically side with the projects and the projects are like, oh yeah, we can't meet standards. But like, from our perspective, I mean like, you might remember, I don't know if you remember this, might be before you got embroiled in this stuff, but like, last year we had a whole bunch of water in the reservoirs like finally, we had a good rain year. And the State asked to violate salinity standards in February. And then like the year before we had no water. And the Feds released a bunch of water to their contractors in in the spring, and then later requested a temporary urgency change petition. Right? So there's a lot of game playing that goes on, and then they make it sound like, oh, babies are dehydrated and aren't getting the water they need. So therefore we can't comply with standards. And it's like, no, you guys game the system, you short the Delta, and then you go cry about it to the board, and the board goes your way. So yeah, we're kind of pissed off.

background.speaker: AD
background.content: Yeah, rightfully.

background.speaker: OM
background.content: We got a bad attitude.

background.speaker: AD
background.content: You pretty much answered my next question, but I'll give you a chance to expand on anything or add anything if you want. But my next question is, are there particular things or phenomena that you would like to see protected in the Delta? And another way of saying, that is, what do you think is most important to protect in the Delta?

background.speaker: OM
background.content: Flows and water quality. And, and cooler temperatures of water to the extent there's an ability to manage that, which it's tough, but you know, that's, that's kind of a HABs connection.

background.speaker: AD
background.content: I haven't heard that one before. That's very interesting.

background.speaker: OM
background.content: Yeah, there's a lot of debate around that, too. About like whether, oh, well, if it gets warmer in a warmer future, you know, is that something that releases of stored water can address, or you know by the time the water comes from, say, Shasta to into the Delta, will it be at air temperature? You know. So anyway, there's, there's a lot of discussion around that. But I, my understanding is that with increased flows at the right times from stored water coming from the bottom of the reservoir in places like Shasta where it's actually cool. With the Sites reservoir, we think that's gonna be like a warm mercury laden mess. But. You know that, yeah, we have, we have more ability to control temperature, I think, than the state and water projects want to admit.

background.speaker: AD
background.content: Gotcha. We have talked about this last question in this block extensively. But maybe if you could just wrap it up in a bow. Can you describe your past and current experience in Delta governance, planning and decision making processes?

background.speaker: OM
background.content: I mean, I've been involved as a advocate in pretty much every single, and that deals with stuff from the Delta, and I probably know all the acronyms in the Delta.

background.speaker: AD
background.content: Well, that's impressive cause I need a scorecard of the acronyms.

drivers_of_change.speaker: AD
drivers_of_change.content: Alright. Well, my next question block is drivers of change. So these questions, basically think of it as how the Delta currently exists now, the status quo, not how it should change in the future cause those will be my next set of questions. So first, what do you think, what factors do you think currently have the most influence on Delta salinity and Delta salinity management?

drivers_of_change.speaker: OM
drivers_of_change.content: Obviously the hydrology. You know. What's happening with the weather. And then how the State and Federal projects are managing their reservoirs.

drivers_of_change.speaker: AD
drivers_of_change.content: If you had to rank them, would you say first is hydrology, and would you include flow rates in that? Or where would you put that?

drivers_of_change.speaker: OM
drivers_of_change.content: Yeah, I mean, I just think, you know. The, the reservoirs aren't supposed to hold back natural flow. I think there's a real question about whether they do or not. There's very little our stream gauging system in the State is in abysmal condition, which is really unfortunate. So it kind of allows DWR and the Bureau to kind of, what they're doing with their management and reservoir storage and releases is kind of a black box. And then they just tell us, like what's going on. And I don't, you know, a reservoir like Shasta has, you know, literally hundreds of creeks flowing into it as well as I think 4 major rivers. So, you know, we do question whether natural flow is always being released. Not sure. But your question was?

drivers_of_change.speaker: AD
drivers_of_change.content: If you had to rank the current factors influencing salinity in the Delta?

drivers_of_change.speaker: OM
drivers_of_change.content: Well, I mean, you know, because of the major reservoirs, you know all the major inflows into the Delta, with the exception of the Cosumnes River is not dammed, right? All the other ones are. So yeah I mean I think the State and Federal water projects along with [?] you've got East Bay MUD operates those reservoirs. But, reservoir operations, probably the biggest factor. I don't know, I hesitate to put that above, you know whether it's a wet year or not, right, because obviously, you know, I do think, yeah, when it gets dry enough, if we're into several years of drought conditions, I mean, it's really, it is quite challenging to figure out like, what could the reservoir operators be doing differently?

drivers_of_change.speaker: AD
drivers_of_change.content: Yeah. How do you anticipate climate change impacting salinity in the Delta?

drivers_of_change.speaker: OM
drivers_of_change.content: Um, I mean, I think the thing I'm most concerned about is really the, the drying. I think it's called like, is it called dessic… There's a d word… Basically runoff is not necessarily what it has been in the past, even with the same amount of rain. And because the earth is more, drier, and it's absorbing more in.

drivers_of_change.speaker: AD
drivers_of_change.content: Okay.

drivers_of_change.speaker: OM
drivers_of_change.content: And so I think that's the factor that… It came up a year or so ago when, this was like 2 years ago, I think when I mentioned yeah, they did a bunch of, you know, releases for contractors. And then, and then, you know, a month later, then DWR is like, oh, there's actually not the amount of snowpack, you know, the snowpack we have up there isn't leading to the amount of runoff we thought it would. And so that's, I guess that's the other thing. So, in addition to like the ground being maybe drier and warmer and not yielding as much runoff as we've expected, I think you've probably seen some studies and stuff using the term like stationary is, you know, dead, or you know, it's not stationary. So, a lot of the ways we manage water is based on how, you know, looking at the past and then trying to, you know, kind of take that past hydrology and then make predictions about what's gonna happen in future. And, you know, those exercises are kind of not helping us adapt or often give us a different answer than what ends up happening in, in real life. More and more, maybe, and it is not just the drying. It's, you know, probably a variety of different things. So I think that's the other thing is that the tools that we have from the past are not necessarily working, you know, to help us plan for the future and ask like DWR, you know the State Auditor last summer it came out with a report that said, yeah, DWR is like, totally not getting it, right, they're totally not adapting. The tools they have are not, as, you know, they're not best avail- I mean, I don't know if they used the term best available science, but seem to be, that was my takeaway is like, look, here's the agency that says it's, you know, got the tools and doing the work to try to manage the resource, and there it is, they're using a lot of outdated stuff, and not like taking in how things are changing. Which again, like, none of us are, you know, we don't know exactly what the future is. But I think we have to try harder, and our state and state entities in particular, [are] kind of fallen down on that. And they're like, oh yeah, we gotta handle. And it's like, no you don't, right? So it doesn't engender a lot of, you know, faith, I guess. But you said, what's the major? So those are 2 challenges. I think, I guess the other challenge I would say with the Delta is just, you know, getting people into like that, the Venn diagram area of where the interests overlap and actually working together for a shared outcome, I think is, because of all the, you know, conflict over specific parts of the whole, it's been very, I think it's very difficult to get, I mean, I think we all kind of do have a similar goal, you know. We'd like to have you know, [...water] for everything to kind of operate well, but, I mean, I think the problem is like for the export interest, you know, they called the Delta Tunnel at Metropolitan, they call it the Delta Solution. Right? So they're thinking, and it's kind of like a religion, is that there's something that could be done infrastructure-wise, that would get them out of having this be a challenge in the future. So, you know, like. You know, I think from my perspective, it's gonna take what they call like an all of the above. Like all these different things are gonna have to happen, [we need] upper watershed work. We need the, you know, we need all these different pieces. And we have to work on everything in this full mosaic. And then hopefully, we can get to a better outcome. It's not, you know, one entity saying like, you know what screw you all. I'll just get what's mine. What I think is mine. I'm just gonna take it. And then the rest of this can just go to hell in a hand basket, like that's, that's the kind of thinking we're dealing with, you know, and they might have nicer words for public discourse. But, that's kind of the plan. And that, that you know, that scares us pretty bad, because, if we be, you know, the Delta itself, like, nobody cares whether farmers and our agencies have what is needed to, you know, continue to be productive. You know again, we're not looking for a handout, but we're looking for the respect and, and legal requirements to be met that were part of the arrangement when it was, I use the term agreed lightly, you know. But that they would put these massive diversions in the south part of the Delta.

drivers_of_change.speaker: AD
drivers_of_change.content: What is most at risk if salinity increases in the Delta?

drivers_of_change.speaker: OM
drivers_of_change.content: I mean, I think it's agriculture, it's communities, and it's, I think a, you know, I mean. It's, it's hard with the Delta smelt, right? Because, like they already are, I mean I think, unfortunately, they, they may be extinct already. I don't think they're what's called extirpated right? And then fish and wildlife is in the process of trying to repopulate the Delta with the smelt that they're growing down at Byron. I don't know, you guys should go to a field trip down there. Look what they do. It's pretty cool, I went on a [redacted] trip down there to look at the tanks where they grow the smelt. It's pretty interesting. But, you know they're trying to repopulate it. But I mean, I think, species are definitely at risk. I don't know the, you know, aquatic species, probably primarily. But it's just, you know, the, the, the salinity regime that has led to the abundance that we had in the Delta, you know, if that changes, it's, it, it has the potential to, and I think it already has kind of upended, you know those food chains and ecosystems.

drivers_of_change.speaker: AD
drivers_of_change.content: What drivers of change would you like to know more about or see studied to help inform salinity management decisions?

drivers_of_change.speaker: OM
drivers_of_change.content: Um… drivers of change… um…

drivers_of_change.speaker: AD
drivers_of_change.content: This could be things like climate impacts that we talked about, extreme wet and dry years, sea level rise, climate warming, the geometry of channels in the Delta, subsidence, tidal marsh restoration. It can be infrastructure, such as levees, hard rock barriers, operable gates. Different water rights and exports and policies.

drivers_of_change.speaker: OM
drivers_of_change.content: Yeah, I mean, I think operable gates are, you know, did you go? Have you seen the, the Bay model? In Sausalito?

drivers_of_change.speaker: AD
drivers_of_change.content: I have not. No.

drivers_of_change.speaker: OM
drivers_of_change.content: You guys should to go for a field trip to that, too. So a long time ago, in the 60s, they're like, yeah, we should just build a gate down there at Carquinez. And so they actually did a Bay model. It's like a, it's in, it's a, I don't know if you can still visit it. It was, it's in Sausalito in an Army Corps building. But, I mean there were fishery concerns with, with the gate, but I mean, I think that kind of solution should probably be looked at. There might be a possibility to put something in like a sill that would still allow for fish migration, but would help, cause what we talk about is, there's kind of like a wedge of salt water that comes in when we have low flows. And so something like that probably is worthy of study, you know. I don't think it should be a substitution for the State and Federal projects, you know, upholding to the extent is possible, which again, is kind of like where the arguments happen is like what's feasible, you know. So, I mean, I think that's another thing I'd like to see studied as a more, a more, some kind of transparent discussion and analysis of what, what is feasible in terms of rest of our operations for maintaining salinity. And then I think we need to, we need to study it, you know, at various levels of, of sea level rise, you know. I think, in the past, and with respect to like what happened with the tunnel project and the EIR there, they assume 1.8 feet of sea level rise, and then they're like oh yeah, the Delta's already, like all salted up, you know. So, really didn't matter to take all that water through the tunnel. You know what I mean. So what I would call gameplaying. Right? So that's why I think, when we talk about sea level rise we have to try to look at different, you know, kind of different, various, variations of it, because honestly, we don't know what, what's gonna happen in the future. So, you know, we should try to plan for some different levels and kind of, we could play around with, you know, what would we do in different scenarios. Rather than kind of doing this Chicken Little the sky is falling therefore, the contractors and the State and Federal Government don't have any responsibilities. Like really?

drivers_of_change.speaker: AD
drivers_of_change.content: Yeah, that's exactly what we're trying to look at with different scenarios, with different levels of extreme drought, no drought, very wet years. So I, I think that's very important.

future_management.speaker: AD
future_management.content: Alright. So these questions are future management and design options. This is about proposed future scenarios. And I think an important note for context, for the project is, we're taking data from the, what we get from the interviews and creating a slew of sample scenarios, maybe 8 or 10, with different conditions. And then we're taking them to, we're having 3 public workshops over the course of the project and so people at the public workshops will up-vote scenarios, down-vote scenarios, and then, from what's decided at the workshops, the different modeling teams on the project will model the impacts. So we don't foresee one specific scenario at the very end, being like this is our Hail Mary scenario. We do still see having 2, 3, maybe even 4 scenarios at the end of everything that, you know, the public thinks are good different interests. So in answering these questions, you don't need like one rock star scenario out of this. So given that, what salinity management strategies do you think are most important or relevant to explore in future scenarios?

future_management.speaker: OM
future_management.content: I think, I mean one of the, for the history of the Central Valley Project at least, it was in part of the justification for it was the drought of the 30s. Right? So I think. And I know the Bureau is… I think the Water Board asked the Bureau to have like a drought management plan. But I mean, I think, coming up with scenarios that look at, you know, that plan for the eventuality of several year droughts, and what can be done with the water storage, you know, with the reservoirs, the Rim reservoirs, and that kind of period is important. Because that was the reason, I mean, that was kind of like the impetus for this, you know at least the first half of, of the, of the Delta project was that, okay, this is gonna help us get through if we have another draw like led to the Dust Bowl. So. Unfortunately, the Bureau and nor DWR have really, we don't think, taken seriously, the necessity to, to plan for, for the longer droughts, you know, cause it's kind of like, oh, one year, 2 year, okay, and then 3 years like, oh my God, we're on fire like, we can't do. Right, so. And I think, 2015, and you know, I mean, and I don't know, I'm not [redacted] or whatever, so I don't really know to the extent it's the droughts are getting longer or not. I mean, I think we're getting drier conditions. You know, for maybe more because of the increased average temperature, you know. It's just drier and hotter and so the water is, you know, not coming when we thought it would. So if that's one thing. So you're looking for… say that question again.

future_management.speaker: AD
future_management.content: Yeah, so different salinity management strategies. So I have a list here as well of different strategies that might be implemented. So this includes changes in water rights, reduced diversions and exports, salinity barriers and/or operable gates, green infrastructure, nature based solutions, restoration which we already talked about a bit, regulatory changes to water quality standards. Other options.

future_management.speaker: OM
future_management.content: Yeah, so, so, yeah, I think about, you know, gaming out water storage options over longer periods. Definitely, I, I do not agree with changing water quality standards. I don't. I mean. I think we need to do the work to see what's possible, you know, and if, but I think the State and Federal water contractors are in way big of, way too big of a hurry to just change the standard like, wouldn't that be great? Well, and that's what they did in South Delta already with Delta Water Board, right? They increase the agricultural water standard because they said that wasn't really being met very much so they might as well increase it. Well of course, people in the Delta didn't think that was a very good idea, you know. So, so, water rights changes, I don't agree with that. I don't see why, and I think this is something that those with what we would call junior water rights are like, oh yeah, let's just change the order. Let's make it so there aren't any senior water rights. I think the most important thing to protect is riparian water rights, because riparian, I have this like an article I want to write. I haven't had time. I keep trying to get like [redacted] to do it, but then, like [redacted], keeps changing. But. So if you know anybody, let me know. But. You know. Riparian water uses, using water near its source where it can provide, you know, you don't lose a lot in, in the, you know, in conveyance, right? And then you have, and you don't, so you're not really wasting anything. Anything that you don't use ends up right back in the system. You know you could talk about runoff and runoff quality and stuff. And that's something, you know, that there's management techniques to address that. So I mean, I think right, people talk about the California water rights system as being antiquated. I don't know. I mean, it's you know, it's the system we have. But I mean, I think retaining riparian rights is, is really important for environmental benefits. You know. summaries.background: The interviewee, aged 52, resides in Sacramento County and Orangeville. They identify as an advocate for various Delta interests and for [redacted]. They have been engaged with the Delta since 2008, initially focusing on local entities and groups concerning Delta matters. Over time, their work has evolved to understand the various regulatory constructs and government entities related to Delta management. Their main takeaway from working in the Delta is the importance of using common sense in resolving issues, especially related to adequate flows. The interviewee stresses the significance of considering local perspectives and engaging with Delta residents in decision-making processes. In terms of future management, they emphasize the need to protect agricultural productivity from increasing salinity and prioritize maintaining adequate flows and water quality in the Delta. The interviewee has been actively involved in Delta governance, planning, and decision-making processes as an advocate for various Delta interests.
summaries.drivers_of_change: The interviewee identified reservoir operations as a primary influence on Delta salinity, expressing concerns about transparency and natural flow management. They also highlighted the impact of climate change on salinity, emphasizing changes in runoff patterns and the inadequacy of existing tools for water management. Additionally, the interviewee suggested exploring the potential of operable gates and studying the implications of sea level rise on Delta salinity to inform better decision-making and adaptation strategies.
summaries.future_management: During the discussion on future management and design options, the interviewee emphasized the importance of planning for longer droughts and exploring water storage options in scenarios. They expressed their stance against changing water quality standards and argued for retaining riparian water rights for environmental benefits, especially in terms of efficiency and wildlife preservation. The interviewee also highlighted the potential of upper watershed restoration to hold water in natural systems longer and suggested exploring impacts of sea level rise on water quality. Additionally, when discussing tunnel conveyance scenarios, the interviewee questioned the operational usage and sea level rise assumptions, emphasizing the need to consider different scenarios to evaluate the tunnel's impacts effectively.
summaries.decision_making: The interviewee criticizes the decision-making process for salinity management in the Delta, highlighting the influence of political pressures that limit the representation of various stakeholders. They believe that the State and Federal water contractors and larger urban areas are represented, while normal Delta farming, environmental groups, fishermen, tribal interests, and disadvantaged communities are not adequately represented. The interviewee suggests connecting with communities in different water service areas, individual farmers, and younger farmers to gather diverse perspectives on Delta issues and ensure a more equitable decision-making process.

So that advocacy from the recreational standpoint, is very immediate. Can I go in the water? Can I catch my fish? And I have this bass tourney right now? And if the answer is yes, the Delta is in good shape. If the answer is no, the Delta is not in good shape that really simplifies and misses out and a lot of opportunities for solutions.

background.speaker: BM
background.content: Yeah that's a good one. Agreed. What do you see as the future of recreation in the Delta? And I guess part of this is, is, how do you think it's changing and will change?

background.speaker: MM
background.content: I hope that this is not the case. But I think that recreation will become much more land-based and less water-based. I think that as conditions proceed along this trajectory, pending decisions to be made, folks will have a very different, different water in the Delta in which to recreate. So I think that things like, it's already been changing, you know, tourism, ag tourism, wine tasting, you know, birding on land and such. I think that that's going to, if it hasn't already, that that's going to be taking over from that traditional sense of being on the water and in the water, just because of everything from invasive plant species like primrose, hyacinth, [?], and you, you name that already has that big impacts. And, you know, water quality, salinity [?] and things like that, that I mentioned, that I sadly think that that is going to really shrink down the opportunities for water-based recreation, and will have people turn towards land-based recreation, which I think is just, it's, would be a sad state of affairs, that you would separate water from recreation in the Delta. That, to me, just seems like a total incongruence. I'm encouraged by restoration opportunities that are going on, by innovative ways at looking at saltwater intrusion, climate change, anything from infrastructure to behavioral stuff, and, and just views. So that is encouraging, you know, increasing flows and things like that. And also, voluntary agreements, I think they have all shown an awful lot of promise. And, but until those things are actually put in place, under an umbrella understanding that this climate change that we have seen is just the first step in that process is going to continue and change things dramatically unless we are taking dramatic steps.

background.speaker: BM
background.content: Yeah. That kind of feeds right into the next question, which I think you've already just partially answered, but how have you been impacted by salinity and the Delta? And you can speak about this professionally, or personally, or both.

background.speaker: MM
background.content: Let's see. So, you know, because professionally, I and my team, staff at [redacted] are really working on interpretation of the Delta, that - it's kind of, this is kind of a rough word to use - but it's kind of a value list or non-advocating point of view that we're just interpreting, and explaining, and connecting people to what's happening. So, salinity intrusion, freshwater blast, that's all those are all equal things to interpret. But as far as personally, I feel like I, you know, in my lifespan, I just missed it, like I just missed out on those incredible wildlife days, mostly in fisheries, you know, by a lifetime. That if I were, if we were to go back 61 years or 62 years from my birthday, 1961, it would have been 1899. And we would have, we would have seen, you know, the beginning of the degradation of the natural Delta that we knew, and reclamation really being in its heyday. But we still had [Antares?] and salmon fishing, and the idea of just walking down to the river and taking a swim. I feel like professionally, it's not so much salinity increased, but just overall quality that I missed out on. And as saltwater continues to move in, that impact is, it's always hard to imagine that within just a couple of my lifetimes, that lifespan, that the Delta will become much more of a saline environment, and how is it that people are going to adapt to that? I'm a little worried about the ability to adapt to increasing salinity and rising sea levels. Engineering-wise, there are plenty of ideas out there. But as far as an overall view of what the Delta is to people, and how accessible it is, when it's saltwater just becomes inherently less accessible. And that, that makes me kind of sad.

background.speaker: BM
background.content: Yeah. Yeah I can see why. This also follows up on that question, are there particular things or phenomena you would like to see protected in Delta? Or another way of saying that is what do you think is most important to predict in the Delta?

background.speaker: MM
background.content: Hmm. Wow, that's a, that's a great question. So let me see, just thinking, is it more like on a cultural side? Are you thinking more on a physical side? Or is it wide open?

background.speaker: BM
background.content: I think it's wide open, you know, okay. Maybe you say it's both or I mean. What do you think?

background.speaker: MM
background.content: I think that overall, it's the, what we do with this physical Delta, is really the most important thing, how are we going to manage the water resources? How are we going to adapt to rising salinity levels? And that can be anything from, you know, I'm not advocating one way or another. But is that a tunnel? Is that increased in-stream flows? Is it, you know, is increased upstream habitat and water storage for environmental uses? You know, all those things. I think there are a lot of things on the table. But what I'm most worried about is that loss of what the Delta is and how we've viewed it over the last 150 years, and I use the 150 years to the Gold Rush, because even though it was colonization before then I see that that, that Gold Rush is really the pivot point in the Delta, where we saw massive, quick changes, but we still have bits and pieces that were, that folks have been able to recreate in as this remnant Delta, this thing that used to be. And so I think that what will be sad was that overall view that the Delta was once a great place to go, recreation haven, wonderful place for fishing, and all the things that recreation provides, into something that people will avoid. Because it's, it takes, it's taken the dive of being inhospitable, it's, it's not safe to go swimming in the water. It's, you don't have those charismatic species, you've got a lot of invasives or non-native species that aren't as attractive for recreation. Water conditions are different. So that overall viewpoint that the Delta has been a recreation haven is something where it's a bit of a mess, a bit of a, almost like a dump. That would be just a shocking change.

background.speaker: BM
background.content: Yeah. Can you describe your past and current experience and Delta governance, planning and decision making processes?

background.speaker: MM
background.content: I've been through work at [redacted] you know, because we're, we're a non-advocating government agency. You know, as far as governance goes, we've advised and educated and interpreted lot of elected officials, water managers, etc. on a number of tours. People will come to [redacted] to learn about the Delta or if we go out in the field. So advising policymakers and advising decision makers on just becoming more aware of the Delta, and the breadth of interests, and impacts of decision. We've also helped with, I've sat on various committees through the [redacted], working with you at [redacted] and the [redacted], I'm sitting on a couple of committees now with the new, the [redacted]. And then this project itself. So on the education side, is our impact our influence on governance at the Delta.

background.speaker: BM
background.content: You're a veteran.

background.speaker: MM
background.content: Yeah, little wee bit now. It's kind of funny how you wake up one morning, like, oh, that's right. I'm one of those old guys now.

drivers_of_change.speaker: BM
drivers_of_change.content: All right. So that's, that's it for the first set of questions. It's probably the, the deepest one. And then now I'm going to switch over into drivers of change. This is again, specific to salinity, but probably crosses over and other things. So the first one is, what factors do you think have the most influence on Delta salinity management? What would you rank as having the greatest potential influence or impact?

drivers_of_change.speaker: MM
drivers_of_change.content: On salinity management?

drivers_of_change.speaker: BM
drivers_of_change.content: Mhmm. This is, there's, so this might just help to clarify, these are the drivers as they currently are. The next, the next set of questions after this are sort of like what are proactive solutions we might think of, and future scenarios, but sort of as things are right now, at this current time, like what do you think have the biggest impact?

drivers_of_change.speaker: MM
drivers_of_change.content: Well, writ large, its climate, but that, the impacts of climate on how we're able to use our infrastructure. So I think right now our, the biggest driver is that we have infrastructure that was built, anticipating a climate would remain the same, a climate that we had over the last 100 years. And now that's different. And we're trying to manage for the same outcome within a whole different system. And so the tools that we've built for ourselves to manage salinity are inadequate now.

drivers_of_change.speaker: BM
drivers_of_change.content: Yeah. So our infrastructure and the ways that we, that all the stuff we have is outdated

drivers_of_change.speaker: MM
drivers_of_change.content: Right.

drivers_of_change.speaker: BM
drivers_of_change.content: Okay. And then, is there anything you put a second, and maybe a third? In terms of influence? Any things below that?

drivers_of_change.speaker: MM
drivers_of_change.content: Oh, sure. Yeah, well, I mean, it's climate. I mean, that's one of the things that we're seeing more frequent, more intensive droughts. And that's probably the biggest thing. And so that's it right now, is over, overall climatological shift with the frequency of longer drought periods, more intense drought periods and such. And so we're trying to so yeah, I'll leave it at that one. And then, so infrastructure, climate, and then we'll just kind of goes with infrastructure, but overall management and political economies. What is it that rules the roost, we can get a, I fear that we have a bit of a whiplash look at the Delta depending on what our economic and political outlooks are, or, or who's in power, that the potential is there that decisions can be made in one for 8, 10 year period, that could direct management in one particular direction, and then you can get in with a whole new set of values and a whole new set of political economies that shifted over to the other direction. And so that that pendulum swing of management back and forth, makes it very difficult to get any kind of consistency. And we tend to view in with that we're trying to manage the Delta as one big homogenous system, when it is not. It's, it's a multitude of small scale ecosystems that are all blended together to make a Delta.

drivers_of_change.speaker: BM
drivers_of_change.content: Yeah. Okay. Yeah, I think my, from what you said, I heard that, you know, there's basically, you know, there's old infrastructure that is built from another time, and there's the interplay with that and climate and how everything is changing. And then feeding into that, or maybe sort of sub, you know, underneath that is just the whole, like, how decisions are being made politically or the different back and forth within the parties. And that sort of swirl of those three is kind of like a, like the dominant drivers that are affecting things.

drivers_of_change.speaker: MM
drivers_of_change.content: Sure, yeah.

drivers_of_change.speaker: BM
drivers_of_change.content: What is most at risk if salinity increases in the Delta?

drivers_of_change.speaker: MM
drivers_of_change.content: Primary among that is the ability to use water, the way we have built up communities throughout the state of California to be dependent on this water. And that when that when the salinity as it continues to increase and becomes more frequent, more intense, that our ability actually use this use the Delta, as an area for water distribution throughout the state, and for protecting and enhancing ecosystems within the Delta, it's going … it's going to be lost. And as we wait, we won't have - because projects and adaptations take a long time, the longer we wait, the less time we have to actually put those things in place.

drivers_of_change.speaker: BM
drivers_of_change.content: What drivers of change, would you like to know more about or see studied to help inform salinity management decisions?

future_management.speaker: BM
future_management.content: Really interesting, okay. Thank you. Alright that's the end of question set number 2. And then, number 3 is really starting to think more about the future, and what our design options might be, so. What salinity management strategies do you think are most important or relevant to explore in future scenarios? And, I think you, you just gave me one, but, go ahead.

future_management.speaker: MM
future_management.content: I guess it really depends on how you define salinity management. If salinity management is keeping saltwater out of the Delta, I think you have limited options. I think that some type of alternative conveyance, a tunnel, canal, pipelines, whatever, it's got to be explored. And, also when we're managing, if we're worried about salinity intrusion, you know, trying to manage for that when we have more tools in the toolbox, which means we would use less water or somehow make more water available upstream to minimize the impacts of salinity intrusion, I think, is, that's a big opportunity as well. Changing the viewpoint there. Can you give me that question again, [redacted]? I think I went off track.

future_management.speaker: BM
future_management.content: No, it's ok. What salinity management strategies do you think are most important or relevant to explore in future scenarios?

future_management.speaker: MM
future_management.content: Okay. So those two, but also looking at…

future_management.speaker: BM
future_management.content: So those two being restoration and alt. conveyance? Are those the two? Or did I miss that?

future_management.speaker: MM
future_management.content: Well I said alternative conveyance, and I had upstream management … water that should go into the Delta, we're starting to see some of that with some more instream flows. But also, restoration and looking at the actual landscape of the Delta that minimizes saltwater intrusion and maximizes the impact for freshwater outflow. So that could be anything from, you know, western islands, things we did, you spearheaded at [redacted], about natural, nature-based barriers to slow down the impacts. Saltwater's coming, but how do we minimize the impacts of that. So looking towards the South and West Delta. I know the North Delta is often spoken about as great opportunities for that. But I would like to see, Western Deltas. Any islands that have the, that we have the opportunity to build up some kind of a saltwater barrier there that just slows down that inevitable rise of sea level and intrusion of saltwater. Really like to see those things hit hard. There's a lot of opportunities in places like Jersey Island, Webb Tract, increasing projects over on Sherman. Big targeted large landscape-scale connected projects to build up nature-based, uh, what's the word I'm looking for… resistance to saltwater intrusion.

future_management.speaker: BM
future_management.content: Mhmm. In some ways, sort of like a scale-up from Franks Tract, if you will, like-

future_management.speaker: MM
future_management.content: A big scale-up of that. Yeah. So that would, yeah, because that's, um, though that's a strategic spot. Um, but, to be able to do that on a much larger scale, that would, I mean it would, that would have some impacts but I'd love to see, you know, negative impacts, but I would love to see some more exploration of that and some more action around that.

future_management.speaker: BM
future_management.content: Mhmm. Great. You know we have a whole list of things that, you know, are possibilities, and some of the other ones we had are, you already covered tunnel and conveyance. We had changes- potential changes in water rights, reduced diversions and exports which I think you were also talking about with like less being diverted up north?

future_management.speaker: MM
future_management.content: Yes.

future_management.speaker: BM
future_management.content: There is also salinity barriers and operable gates. You talked more about, you know, nature-based, which we also have on here. And then regulatory changes to water quality standards which I think gets back to your original comment of like, you know, like, the D-1641, the TUCPs and things like that, that we're seeing, you know, being used more often, so I guess maybe some of my questions here, do you see anything around water rights or regulatory changes or anything that should be explored there?

decision_making.speaker: BM
decision_making.content: Mhmm. Great. Okay. Last set of questions. Decision making and who should be involved. Tell me what you worked on, this one is more qualitative in how these things happen. How would you describe decision making regarding salinity management in the Delta? And then sort of the sub question to that is, do you consider these processes equitable and fair? Why or why not?

decision_making.speaker: MM
decision_making.content: Boy.

decision_making.speaker: BM
decision_making.content: We're good on time, so take your time, too.

decision_making.speaker: MM
decision_making.content: Yeah, they're certainly - I don't consider them equitable. Fair is kind of a different story. I think that you, somebody as I mentioned earlier on, when decisions are made regarding salinity intrusion, somebody's gonna get screwed. Even if you're successful 95% of the time and you don't exceed salinity limits, but that 5% of the time is a story we would tell in a big way. Let's just say that 5% of the time happened when you have somebody who's putting on a bass tournament, you know, is counting on freshwater, and when there's a little saltwater blast that comes up just enough to move the bass upstream, it's a bust of a tournament, nobody comes back, and economically somebody really gets screwed that way. That could be a fair thing, like it seemed to be very successful, that there's 95% of the time we're making our water quality requirements. But that 5% of the time can really be ruinous for some people. So. I don't consider that to be equitable. That's a tough one. And can be really unfair. Overall, considering the statewide importance of the Delta, that right now I think a lot of people look at it as it's not equitable because I don't think they see, they might be intellectually aware, but they don't have that everyday feeling of what the impact would be if a particular management process took hold. So if you are a farmer in the San Joaquin Valley, what you consider equitable and fair is to get your full allotment that you need to reach your particular goals. If you're a salmon fisher on the coast, you have a very different idea there. So … as far as processes going forward, it's a big, big process because so many people depend on it. So all the standard players that we have now, ag interests, urban water users, environmental folks, all, you know, that's all fine. I think the folks that we're losing out on are people who just aren't as tuned into those things. So a big one, local communities around the Delta is the, it's huge. I mean, think of someplace like Stockton. And when you have people who are doing subsistence fishing, or they're riding their jet skis or whatever, and they're just not even aware that there are harmful algal blooms. Or that there might be certain levels of toxicity in particular fish and they're bringing that home to feed their families because there are language barriers, there are cultural barriers. It's those… I think that the big players, they have their interests pretty much locked up. They're gonna, they're gonna be able to profess their interests. It's the smaller players that really define the Delta, we think about the charm and the beauty of the Delta as these small communities. What kind of say and involvement do those small communities have? How much time do they have, how many resources do they have to actually go to a public hearing, read through documents and things like that, and come up with some kind of a decision that they can feel is well-informed? I don't, I'm not convinced that we have that.

decision_making.speaker: BM
decision_making.content: Mhmm. Thanks, yeah you kind of went right into the next question, so I think I have most of that, but I just want to see if you want to add to it. The next question was who do you think is represented, and who is not? So I got from who's represented so far is you talked about ag interests and water users, and I think environmental?

decision_making.speaker: MM
decision_making.content: Yeah, and environmental, yeah.

decision_making.speaker: BM
decision_making.content: Yeah. Go ahead, go ahead.

decision_making.speaker: MM
decision_making.content: Yeah so those folks are, are, have great interest, but yeah it's the smaller communities and people around who don't. I think that you can go up and down the state and, although you might have, you hear about Westlands or Kern County or something like that. Water users, you know these larger groups. But what about these smaller communities, farm workers and such. All these folks that really bear the brunt when there are water cutbacks or quality problems, or something like that, that there are these, you know, who is it that's really getting hammered on these things? And I think that the larger interests ultimately, they hold enough sway back and forth that they're, they feel like they have a chance to make an impact. I feel like, and this is just a gut feeling, [redacted], that there are a lot of folks who are completely left out of this discussion who have the most immediate impacts. You're telling somebody, in, again, say in Stockton, that you can no longer fish along the banks here, and you're doing good work because the fish aren't safe to eat. How is it they're actually going to end up getting food then? How are they going to keep up their cultural practices of, you know, good Catholics, fish on Fridays, we caught that, we're going to eat it tonight. You know, those are impacts that we don't really, we don't hear enough about.

decision_making.speaker: BM
decision_making.content: Mhmm. Yeah, goes back to I think what you said about the experiential versus the sort of more abstract intellectual quality of the decision making.

decision_making.speaker: MM
decision_making.content: Right.

decision_making.speaker: BM
decision_making.content: Yeah. Well, if you could wave your wand, how do you think decision making could be improved?

decision_making.speaker: MM
decision_making.content: Boy. I've been a big advocate in, you could say 4th grade, 5th grade, 6th grade, whatever it is. You know, 4th grade you have, you know, the Missions in California. That's one of the requirements that all the kids learn. It could be in high school or whatever, but I think that a comprehensive water curriculum for kids in school is a big one. And that overall management decision making should automatically recognize all the different people who might be impacted. So that means a real diversity of language, and a broader understanding of cultures and how they view authority, how they view management, how they view government, how they feel their particular safety in a place. You know, anybody from who's just been told to respect authority, to somebody who may be, you know an undocumented worker who is living here, and they're fearful of expressing their opinions. So overall, waving that magic wand would be to make water an everyday part of every Californian's experience, not just through putting out websites and PSAs and things like that, but have it become a part of California culture starting with education.

decision_making.speaker: BM
decision_making.content: Great. Follows up on what you've already talked about, but maybe you have some specifics, I don't know, but what people, stakeholders, and vulnerable communities do you think we should contact with respect to this study? If you have any specific ideas on that.

decision_making.speaker: MM
decision_making.content: Hmm. Gee whiz. [...] Talked about some of them. I'm thinking of, of folks outside of the Delta. People who could be impacted by particular management decisions, being, you know, farmers, leaning more- when you talk about vulnerable communities, I think more of like seasonal folks, farm workers, people living closer to the poverty level, people who are food insecure, folks who have strong cultural attachments to the Delta that they may have brought from other parts of the world or they just grew up with here. Gee whiz. I think I've probably touched on a lot of these things already [redacted].

decision_making.speaker: BM
decision_making.content: Mhmm. No it just was if there were specific ones or ways you think we should try to bring this stuff into the study.

decision_making.speaker: MM
decision_making.content: I think that overall within the Delta, we're seeing a bit more of a proliferation of culturally identified groups. An example would be, is it Manila, no it's not Manila Rising. There's a group, Filipino group in Stockton.

decision_making.speaker: BM
decision_making.content: Little Manila Rising?

decision_making.speaker: MM
decision_making.content: Little Manila Rising. Yeah, that's it, yeah. So that's one group. Looking along the northern shoreline of Contra Costa County. You know, cities that have particular interests in water, because they're right on there and they get their water from there and such, but some of those other communities that even though they're right next to the Delta, the community itself, that they don't have any idea of what's there. So, looking out to particular groups from Baypoint, Pittsburgh, Antioch, there's a lot of community groups there. […] and over in the eastern county too, Eastern Contra Costa County. Not as familiar with particular groups going up into the northern Delta. I think that, you know, possibly, I don't know if we've really heard much about union groups. You know, United Farm Workers, or other work groups that have strong dependency on water policy. I'm not as familiar with those, though.

decision_making.speaker: BM
decision_making.content: Okay.

decision_making.speaker: MM
decision_making.content: Yeah. And just community, community-based organizations in farming areas up and down the Valley.

decision_making.speaker: BM
decision_making.content: Thank you. Well, that concludes the questions we have. I think I, in closing, ask you, related to what you know about the project and what we're doing, anything I didn't ask, or that you want to speak to or anything you think was left out or any points that you want to contribute? Or anything else?

decision_making.speaker: MM
decision_making.content: Yeah. What I found to be an interesting aspect of a lot of projects that there's an assumption that folks are understanding the problem in the first place. That you know, when you say there's saltwater coming in, that could be a big problem. Why is that happening? What is the cause and effect? What are some of the different things, that, the impact of the different strategies and such? I learned that a lot through, you know, Delta Conveyance. That there was a very limited focus to what folks can talk about and present for that project through DWR. It's very limited, it's only this, it's not attached to any other projects here. So to, I'm just imagining if we brought folks together into [?] Community Center in [redacted], and we talked about salinity intrusion, you know, what is some of the concerns people might have, what are some equitable solutions? I mean a lot of folks just don't know a lot of the language or why things have happened to really get that baseline knowledge of what has happened in the Delta in the last 150 years, what have been the impacts. It's difficult, it's complex, but I think it's necessary to have some kind of a common baseline understanding of things that have happened in the Delta, impacts over time, and you know, why people are even in the visitor's, in the community center in the first place. Why is saltwater coming in? Why is that happening? Why is this a concern, this is a freshwater area. So that baseline over, and that could be the interpreter, the educator in me, that I think like everybody's gotta have that baseline understanding of the issues and how we got there before we can come up with any kind of solution that might adequately or comprehensively address the issues.

decision_making.speaker: BM
decision_making.content: Mhmm. That's helpful. Yeah, it's a hard thing to do, because as you say it's so complicated, and there's a lot of people who don't, I mean, so many people don't know the full, a lot of the history of the Delta. Or it's kind of invisible in some ways, it's just there.

decision_making.speaker: MM
decision_making.content: Right.

decision_making.speaker: BM
decision_making.content: Mhmm. Cool. Thank you. I'm gonna try to turn my camera on, see what happens.

decision_making.speaker: MM
decision_making.content: Alright, sounds great.

decision_making.speaker: BM
decision_making.content: It's working.

decision_making.speaker: MM
decision_making.content: So is there anything else that I missed? Hi [redacted], I'm [redacted].

decision_making.speaker: AD
decision_making.content: Hi [redacted], I didn't want to interrupt you. Nice to meet you, I'm sorry my plane was a little delayed, but I'm back in Davis now. And I'll listen to the recording later today, but from what I caught it was some very thought-provoking comments and very interesting.

decision_making.speaker: MM
decision_making.content: Well thank you, thanks. Well if I, I mean do you feel like, did I gloss over anything [redacted], did I miss anything?

decision_making.speaker: BM
decision_making.content: No I thought your answers were really, really thoughtful and spoke to your experience and everything you've been doing in the Delta. I mean if you have any follow-up thoughts or anything we missed, feel free to get in touch.

decision_making.speaker: MM
decision_making.content: Okay.

decision_making.speaker: BM
decision_making.content: I liked your last one a lot, I think there is, you know, part of this project is hopefully getting at education about these issues, and, you know, because it's, or why, or what one management thing means, or really like, how these different things, I guess it goes back to what you initially started with of like, you talked about recreation and like people, if you only look for your interest, then you kind of forget the others, and that's kind of what we're trying to do with the project is to show if you have this attachment with the Delta, you might get impacted this way, but so and so over here is getting impacted this way, and to try to understand the different ways that those happen at a larger thing I thought was really, really, like a strong point there as well. So no I thought you, it was really helpful, really, really interesting to hear.

decision_making.speaker: MM
decision_making.content: Yeah I think overall the word that I've used over the years is empathy. That there, that people have a vested interest in not being empathetic. Because when you're an advocate, it's very effective to know what's empathetic and to answer it or resist it or refute it before you could actually feel it and act upon it. And I think that's what, it seems like that's what this project is doing, is opening up a lot more empathy to all these different folks that are impacted and depend by decisions about the Delta and depend on it, and I'd be very curious to see if you know there's this [?] of small interest, you know, of interest groups, small group of interest groups, but what if everybody had a say? What if everybody actually gave their opinion? Would it be different? It's kind of like, what if everybody voted? What would the outcome actually be?

summaries.background: The interviewee has over 30 years of experience in the Delta, progressing from a naturalist to a supervising naturalist, and now a regional manager. Through education and interpretation, the interviewee has learned the importance of maintaining an open mind and avoiding narrow perspectives, which can limit understanding and potential solutions for the Delta's complex issues. They emphasize the need for a holistic view and worry that a narrow focus on particular interests might overlook broader, multi-benefit solutions. summaries.background: Having engaged with the Delta for the past 12 years as a researcher and resident, the interviewee underscores the unity within Delta communities in their advocacy and political engagement on issues affecting the region, from agriculture to water quality and social justice. They highlight that the Delta's agricultural landscape is adapting continuously, citing changes in crop patterns, technological advancements like drip irrigation, and a growing interest in crops like rice that help to mitigate subsidence. The interviewee also speaks to their professional experiences with salinity through soil surveying and policy presentations, believing that understanding and conveying scientific information about salinity is a crucial part of their work. As a member of various steering committees and working groups, the interviewee actively contributes to Delta governance and planning processes, emphasizing the importance of protecting water quality for the Delta's economy and beneficial uses.
summaries.drivers_of_change: During the interview, the interviewee stresses that drought and reduced water flows are the most impactful factors on Delta salinity, based on their firsthand experiences. Climate change, sea-level rise, and tidal influences are also considered important, although there is an acknowledgment of the difficulty in planning for sea-level rise due to uncertainties around its progression. Water movement throughout the state and subsequent reuse, as well as the economic valuation of water in decision-making, are discussed as factors influencing salinity. Regulatory compliance and the enforcement of water quality objectives are noted as areas affecting salinity management. The interviewee is hesitant to rank the impact of these factors but suggests that agriculture is most at risk from increased salinity, while urban areas may face less severe, albeit impactful, challenges.
summaries.future_management: The interviewee highlighted the importance of better monitoring and mapping to understand the distribution of salts in waterways for effective salinity management. They also mentioned the success of the False River barrier in keeping salts back during droughts and expressed interest in nature-based solutions for salinity control. Additionally, the interviewee emphasized the need for improved coordination and communication among different agencies and programs to address environmental issues holistically. They emphasized the interconnectedness of various aspects like water use, agricultural landscapes, and salinity, calling for a more integrated approach in managing these complexities.
summaries.decision_making: The interviewee indicates decision-making around salinity management in the Delta as critical but currently unfair due to the failure to meet relevant objectives, pointing to a deficit in shared commitment. Representation includes various agencies, water contractors, and some advocacy groups, yet being represented does not necessarily equate to being heard. There's criticism of the stakeholder engagement process, which often feels like a box-ticking exercise rather than a meaningful and empathic dialogue. Improvements should focus on listening and engaging with stakeholders in good faith, including those directly affected such as private landowners. The interviewee refrains from identifying additional contacts for stakeholder engagement, suggesting familiarity with the relevant groups on the interviewer's part.

The interviewee has not specified a third most influential factor but suggests a combination of dry and wet years also contributes to the issue. summaries.future_management: During the discussion on future management and design options to manage salinity in the Delta, the interviewee highlighted Indigenous sovereignty and water rights as crucial strategies, emphasizing the importance of giving back Indigenous rights. When asked about their ranking, the interviewee prioritized Indigenous sovereignty and water rights first, followed by marsh restoration and subsidence reversal. summaries.decision_making: In the interviewee's view, decision-making related to the salinity management in the Delta is complex and might not be fully equitable or fair, potentially due to inadequate representation and engagement of all those affected by the Delta's conditions. summaries.background: The interviewee, a 49-year-old individual residing in Forest Ranch, with Zip code 95942, identifies as having a mixed Native American and White heritage. They describe their relationship with the Delta as deep, central to their culture as a Plains Miwok person. Their engagement with the Delta dates back to childhood, spending weekends at a family property in the South Delta and forming intimate knowledge of the area. Over the years, their involvement evolved to include a focus on the intersections between water management, recreation, agriculture, and the environment, particularly in their early career roles at different organizations. They have been actively engaged in discussions around water management, environmental concerns, and tribal perspectives in the Delta, collaborating with various organizations and taking on leadership roles to advocate for a better future for the Delta, bridging cultural perspectives with science.
summaries.drivers_of_change: The interviewee emphasizes the significant influence of State and Federal Water Projects on Delta Salinity management, controlling water flow to keep saltwater out. Climate change, including sea-level rise and shifts in precipitation, is also considered a crucial factor affecting saltwater intrusion. Additionally, the increasing water demand due to population growth, changing agricultural practices, and industrial usage is viewed as a key driver that could impact Delta salinity in the future.
summaries.future_management: The interviewee emphasized the importance of exploring salinity management strategies in future scenarios. They suggested allowing salinity to vary over time and reconnecting islands in the Delta to potentially change the influence of saltwater in the region. The interviewee also discussed the idea of structural landform changes to alter salinity pathways and create habitat, as well as closing gaps between land formations to impact salinity levels. These strategies aim to address the current salinity challenges in the Delta and restore connectivity to better manage salinity distribution.
summaries.decision_making: The interviewee raised concerns about the lack of fairness in the decision-making process in the Delta, pointing out the historical exclusion of indigenous peoples and marginalized communities. They highlighted the importance of including grassroots individuals and tribal people at the decision-making table to provide diverse perspectives. The interviewee also emphasized the need for open discussions to welcome innovative ideas from overlooked voices.

summaries.background: The interviewee, a 31-year-old tribal member with cultural ties to the Delta, shared their deep connection to the waterways and gathering sites that hold significant cultural importance to their community. They expressed concerns about the protection of these sites from overexposure and discussed the impact of introducing others, both tribal and non-tribal, to these sacred locations. Looking towards the future, the interviewee emphasized the importance of working collaboratively with tribes to manage cultural resources sustainably and educate both tribal and non-tribal members on cultural practices. They highlighted the need to preserve the natural flow and environment of the Delta, suggesting initiatives such as reintroducing native plants and creating more Tule beds to restore the ecosystem. The interviewee expressed personal impacts from salinity changes in the Delta, noting how controlled environments disrupt natural processes and affect cultural resources, emphasizing the importance of working harmoniously with the land for a sustainable future.
summaries.drivers_of_change: The interviewee emphasizes the importance of managing Delta salinity to protect resources and preserve the ecosystem. They express concerns about the potential risks to current resource availability and highlight the decline in key species like the delta smelt and salmon as indicators of the negative impacts of inadequate management practices. This underscores the need for improved strategies to mitigate salinity levels and safeguard the Delta's ecological balance.
summaries.future_management: The interviewee emphasized the importance of increased tribal involvement in decision-making processes regarding salinity management in the delta. They expressed a desire for more information sharing and communication to better understand and participate in project plans and future endeavors along the delta. The interviewee also mentioned a need for better awareness and time allocation from the state and Delta steward to ensure equitable and inclusive decision-making processes.
summaries.decision_making: The interviewee highlighted the involvement of tribal patrimony in the decision-making processes in the Delta, indicating a fair level of representation. The interviewee did not specify any groups that are not represented and suggested that the decision-making process could be improved by considering tribal patrimony.

Sometimes they're bad, but they're not preventing people from operating, but because of the export pumps rather than the water going through the Delta channels and making its way out from the South Delta.
